title: Going out and returning in Pharoah's music; buying his bass
summary: On Prince of Peace and group freedom, and the bass he bought on 42nd Street two weeks before Thembi.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: Right. I just was listening to some of that kind of thing, and there was a tune, “Prince of Peace”
And the overall quality of it is fairly peaceful but at around ten minutes —
I know what you’re going to say.

You’re talking about things that can spring out of people. And it shocked me and honestly it’s rather frightening until it’s just — I’m wondering if you remember that specifically and do you believe that Pharoah expected the accompanists to go with him?

Absolutely. Absolutely. Now that you have provided assurance that what is taking place currently is secure in terms of its intent to express, it’s all right to go there now. Because you’ve provided that premise from which it comes. See? So in performance it’s okay to go out there because you’ve done so well which causes for you to feel that it’s okay to go out there that you know in leaving where you were, the memory of that prevails. So you can just do what you want you know, and play collectively, everybody’s listening and adhering to the rules of tone placement, of harmonic placement, rhythmic let’s say, what’s the word —

Interaction. Yeah. And so you are out there, you are doing your thing only to return to where you came from or either let it go. For instance, speaking of Pharoah the current bass that I have now, which I’ve had since then, this is 1969. My principal bass, I have one other, I had gone into a store on 42nd Street between Sixth and Seventh Avenues in New York, but it was a bass shop, to get some strings. And there were three basses on a rack. And the first bass really appealed to me. It had the shape and curves that just were wonderful, past what I had experienced before, just like an upgrade. So I played it and fell in love with it and ended up buying it. Right? And so that was two weeks before we recorded “Thembi.” So in the studio we were going to play this tune, and Pharoah being somewhat unpredictable at times in terms of what he would play, when he would play, and how he would play, you had to go with that. He said, “Hey, look, let McBee play something out front and then we’ll come in at Letter A at my cue.” Right? So I just started playing. And this was a tune called “Love” that to this day in my travels around the world people were very very appreciative of my quality of expression, my quality of thought.
